blocks.x: I'll give you a name so we'll have your name down.
My name is Lewis Geller.
We're recording this, is it 1630?
North Villaray.
North Villaray. On May the 18th of the day.
18th, yeah.
Could you tell just when you were born and what part of town?
I was born in New Orleans, Louisiana, February 27th, 1897. I know all the musicians in the city mostly.
Did your father, mother, anyone in the family play anything?
No, they didn't play anything that I knew of. They never played anything.
Any brothers or anyone else in the family that played?
Played anything. No, they didn't play anything. But I know a lot of musicians that played with me.
Can you remember the very first music you ever heard? Which bands when you were a little boy as far back as you can remember?
I heard that at the Palm Garden. I wasn't a little boy when I was four years old. I was around in the 20s, something, in the 20s, I think.
Where was the Palm Garden?
On Grab and Rampart.
Oh, yeah.
On top of the building. Oh. It's there now where Joe Peck is, I think it is now. Yeah, where Joe Peck is. It's because he didn't ramp up that. No, Grab and Rampart.
On the top floor?
Yeah, on the top floor. Who was the top floor?
Was it that the Pithian Temple or?

No, it wasn't the Pithian Temple. The roof garden up there. I remember the roof garden too. Not that place. Not that place. It was on over the, right on Grab and Rampart. Right on the upstairs. Up there. And on the Padilla Rampart, I played there at the Golden Slipper. We punched.
And played at the next place.
And played at the next place. We played at the Ruby Restaurant at Little Woods. And played at Lutton.
When did you take up music? How old were you about when you started?
When I started to play, I was around in 21. 21. 27, something like that. 21, something like that. 21, something like that. 21.
Now, was piano your first instrument?
Piano was the first instrument. From that I'd taken up banjo, you see?
You'd never played anything else before? Never did play anything else before.

Piano was the first instrument. Never did play anything else before. But Rene and them would come to the house and teach me, you know? Show me how to play. And also, Kid Howard and Morgan, Andrew Morgan and all of them. And they had one boy, a fella there they called Wayback 2, had a little short horn. His name was Chris Kelly. Oh, yes. And Dauphine, you know, also in the same block as Kid Rene, on Dauphine there, Domingue, between Domingue and Phillip, rather. And, let's see, yeah.
You had a piano at your house?
Yeah, I had a piano at my house. I always did have a piano, you know?
Did you tell just what part of town you were born in and where you were raised and where

you lived? I was born in the back of town section around Taunty and Sedan, where I was born. And I was raised up around the back of White and Tupre and Lopez and Arlene. You know, got married two years before the war, before the war won.
Did you say Kid Rene lived down on Dauphine?

Yeah, him and his mother and his brother. Later he lived there. Later he lived there. When they had a dinner there, when Gaillet was playing trombone with him there. And the Burn West went big out when they begged him to go away when Louis Armstrong went away. They wanted him to go away also, but he didn't want to leave town. Otherwise he'd have been way up in the world, you know? He wouldn't mind being there.
What was your first job? Do you remember when that first job?

The first job I played was at this, was at, let's see, by Ben Mulligan for the George. Well that was for George, Joan and, well, Horst was there, but we used to call him Manuel Minetta. He used to play there too. And I used to come there and play there too at Judge Ben Mulligan on Grab and Rampart. They used to have the judge and all we used to entertain the judge. And then, you know, late watchmen. Was that near the Palm Garden?
Where was, it was just the saloon, was it?
It was the saloon, and this is like a saloon. They used to dance in there now.
Which side of the street was that on?
On the uptown side and the back of town side. Up and back down.
Is that where the Pelican was later? Where the Pelican was.
That's where Ben Mulligan used to be.
He was right in the old building with the Pelican?
The Pelican was. Before they knocked it down, that's been a long run.
Yeah.
And I used to play up in there for the judge and all, Captain Smith and all that.
Which judge was that?
That was Judge LeBlanc. And I think he had no legs on the last, after a while I heard he had lost his legs. He's dead now, I know.
What did Manuel Minetta play?
Oh, he played the piano. He played two different songs, you know, when he chants. He played two different songs. He played a song with each hand. Well, he still does that sometimes.
Dixie and what's the other one? Yankee Doodle.

Yankee Doodle. Yeah, that's the two numbers he played then. But he used to be there when we used to come and play. Well, George Jones used to play the bass and sing again at the time. That's where we used to play all out Millenbury for Nick Voyages, Philly Voyages and them, the price battle. We used to play out there. They had a place on the lake at Millenbury and we played out there.
Who was leader of the band? Out there?

Yes. Well, I was leading the band out there because I had, who I was there playing with me was Cripple Voynell and Cripple Voynell and Edward Johnson across the street. He's old now. I don't think he played anymore. What's his name?
Edward Johnson. Noon? Not Noon.
No, Edward Johnson. He played saxophone. We had in the Cripple Voynell. Do you know him? Cripple Voynell?
No, I don't think so.
He used to hop around the drum and run with him and make a run. He's had a Cripple Foot. He went to, last time I heard from him, he was in North, you know, Alexander.
Mr. Jones is still living then. Yeah, he's over there. We'll have to try to talk to him sometime.
He's going to play no more, but.
We'd still like to talk to him, you know, because he'd remember, could tell us about
his life. Johnson. Yeah, he can tell you about it. Johnson.
I used to play with him too, you know.
Well, let's say Jones. After Johnson, I mean. Eddie Johnson. Oh, yes, I've heard of him.
You know him? Eddie Johnson. I've heard of him, yes.
You know Santiago? Yes. Well, that's his brother-in-law. That's his brother-in-law. I was mixed up.
You were talking about Jones was the bass player.

Oh, yeah, that's George Jones. He used to get all the jobs around there and play. That's the time, that's the old time. He used to play guitar and bass too and sing, you know. He was in a, during the time, Cornelius, Washington, and them used to have a, all them cabarets around, uh, uh, Basin and, uh, in Bienville. Basin and Bienville by Louis White there. And, uh, he used to play in that place there. And I used to play for Harris Stilley too at Countdown in Bourbon. And also at Corndown in St. Louis for Harris Stilley. He died. What was his last name?
Stilley.
Stilley.
Stilley.
Mm-hmm. Little bit of short-filling. Cabaret.
Cabaret then.
Cabaret. When Buddy Bertrand was with it, eh? And, uh, let's see who was there with me then. Uh, we had, uh, clean drum.
I've heard of a Buddy Bertrand, uh, Jolly Roll, um,

Yeah, he was, he played piano too. He played piano too. He died some time ago. He used to be around 25 all the time. He used to play piano around there sometime. And when we used to get off, I used to go around there. Well, I used to have a violin player there, Willie Dan's boy. Oh, yeah. Playing violin from Baton Rouge. He's in Baton Rouge. He was sick some time ago. I tried to find him. But he used to come here. Well, he's in Baton Rouge. You think he's still up there then? Yeah, he's still living. He still was at the hospital down here. I don't know if he's living yet. I never heard nothing. We tried to find him last year.
We were trying, we didn't never, didn't find anybody.

Well, I'm gonna try to get in touch with him, you see, because he used to play with me and he used to get all that job and work around. I'd like to talk to him sometime. All around Bourbon Street, that was our wait quarters. All around that we used to play.
Go back to Buddy Berkman. You said he was a waiter.
He's a waiter and he used to play piano too. He played the piano.
And wait on too.

But we used to play in the same place. At the same time. Same job. Yeah, when we wouldn't be there, you know, he used to play. And he used to be a waiter. He was a first class waiter. Do you know where he came from?
Anything about him? I don't know anything about him.
Yeah, he used to live on, he used to live around Krause there on, on North Ferry between, let me see now, North Ferry. He's right by Krause there used to live, right across from Krause.
You're pretty sure he's dead then now?
Yeah, he's dead. I know he's dead. He died around, he died about four years ago or something like that.
Is that all?
Mm-hmm.
Do you think he came from New Orleans or someplace else? Yeah, he's from New Orleans. He's been here all his life.
He's been here all his life. He's been, all he's been doing is waiter and food with the piano. Mm-hmm.
Didn't know if he came like from Mobile or Florida or something like that?
No, he came from right here. Right here. He came from right here, Bradenum, right here. And, uh…
Any other old time pianist like that that you can remember when you were…
Old time pianist? Well, I knew, uh, Udill. You remember Udill.
I never met him. Udill Wilson was that…
I think he's dead.
I think so too, yeah.

He had his, his daddy was a preacher. I think he come from, uh, he was born in, uh, what's the name of that place again? Memphis. That's where he come from. And he went back to Memphis and he died. That's the last job they played when, which, uh, Lee Collins. Oh, yes. Lee Collins played there. I knew of a years ago. That's the 101 they called it, but it was, uh, and they called it the Entertainer. And they called it the 101.
Did you play there with, uh, that group ever?

No, I used to pass there and, uh, talk to them and stay there and hang around there. When I used to get off, stay there all night hanging around there with them and leave there and go eatin', you know, and breakfast and stuff. I know them though. They always livin' around where I was livin'.
Who was about the best pianist? Did you, did you have any favorite, any choice of all the fellas you heard when you were young?

Well, the best pianist in that time that I think was, uh, Professor Mineta. Professor Mineta. Yeah, because he was on the boat, you know, at the corner of the boat. And he was the only one playin' that, that organ, you know, at that time. And I used to love to hear that carrier for the car. He used to play that. Then Fat Pichon come in there, you know. Yeah. But he used to be the one that had that job. Mm-hmm. Here with his band. Him and I think it was, uh, Peter Bocard was on there. When you. I think it was at the, and then Walter Deku, he was at the country club there at that time. That's it. Him and the Bocard.
Were there any other favorite pianists that were unusually good that you liked?

Well, at that time, mm-hmm. There was a lady piano player playin' on the roof garden. And, uh, at that time when I was a boy, when I used to go up there when I was a young man, a young boy, I used to go up there and dance. Before I started to playin', I used to go up there when, uh, Manuel, uh, Peris was playin' up on the roof. Mm-hmm. On the roof garden with, uh, Big Eye Louie and Caffrey. And that lady, what's her name again, uh, let's see if I can call her name.
But I knew they had a clan that play a playin' up there.
They called, uh, what's the name? Uh, Sherry, Eddie Sherry at that time. Eddie Sherry, yeah. And Manuel, uh, uh, what's her name again? Manuel. Manuel. Perez. And Big Eye Louie. And, uh.
Who was the trombone, you remember?

Oh, yeah. Let's see now who's that trombone. I know him in the crown skin. See how the colors, and, uh, I can't tell you, but I knew him. I knew that name. If I could've just, I got books in there that got that, but I don't.
There was, uh, one fella used to play with, uh, Manuel Perez's George Field for a while. No, but I don't remember him.

Did Buddy Johnson ever work with him? They had a brown skin fella they called, uh, used to play with him then. Um, Ducey. Ducey. Ducey. Frankie Ducey. Frankie Ducey. Frankie Ducey. Oh, Frankie Ducey. Yeah, Frankie Ducey. He was playing with them too. Did you ever hear Dutre? Nori Dutre they called him.

Played Cranet? No, uh, trombone. He was with Joe Oliver later. He left here pretty early though. I think he'd never played here much after he was. But I mean, is he akin to Dutre the Tranny, please? Yeah, Sam Dutre. Yeah, Sam. He was his brother. Oh yeah, well I remember Sam Dutre, but I don't remember him.
I guess Nori, the trombone that's left here when he was pretty young. Is his name again? Uh, playing trombone too. He was a good trombone player too.
Uh, this fella, uh, this fella's name again.
Used to have that ballroom on the corner grabbing him. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm.
Mm-hm.
Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
I can't think.
Ridley, Ridley.
Oh yeah, Bebe Ridley.
Bebe Ridley, that's right.
He's out in Carleton now.
We've talked to him.
He still seems to be healthy now. He was sick a while, but he's…
Yeah, I got operated on above. Me, I got operated on in March the 15th. Just last? The 58.
I remember hearing you were sick there once, but I didn't know.
I was very sick. I'd like to win. I got a big cut and I suffer with it now most of the time.
I'm going to ask about Joe Oliver. If you remember his band and hearing Joe when you were a kid?

Oh yeah, I heard his band. He used to play around at the, he played at the Carparetus Hall. He played at the Connemy Hall. Of course Buddy Petey and them used to play there too. He played with his buddy Petey and Kid Punch, Rainey.
Who was the best trumpet players in those days that you liked best? At that time?

Yeah. Well, Sam Morgan I think had the best band at that time. Sam Morgan, then Rainey. And Sam Morgan had the best band for a reading band, you know. But a jazz band I think Buddy Petey used to draw a crowd and Rainey too.
How did Buddy Petey play? What style did he… Oh, he had a funny style.
He had a nice style. He had a nice style.
And he like anybody today that you can think of?
Oh, I don't hear nobody today play like him. Buddy Petey had a style of his own. Some people… Also Rainey too, yeah.

Some people said that Armstrong played something like Buddy Petey. Not now so much when he, Louie hits a lot of high notes. But I mean some of Louie's style, some people say it's something like Buddy Petey. Do you remember? Louis Armstrong? Yeah, would you say there's any comparison or?

Well, if you'd say some pieces he played, some pieces he played. Some pieces. Yeah, some pieces he played sounds like him, them low down pieces like he used to play. Well at that time the rather music, the jazz, the more jazz you put to it the better you was at that time. Of course the nicer music you'd play you wouldn't be nothing at that time, you know, because people liked it plenty of jazz. But it's like they go for plenty of stuff now, but that used to be real music they used to play. Sure. It'd be hard music, but plenty of it they never put it in music. We had lots of music, lots of pieces we ain't never heard. They ain't never like this number about all the wrong you did to me and all them pieces. But Buddy Petey used to play all of that. You see I ain't never heard these other bands play all of that.
No, I don't hear them anymore now.
They certainly coming back to me and if you don't want me to know, make me a pallet on the floor and all them numbers, well they used to play all of that. You see.
But these mother bands they didn't play none of that because they was, I don't know, their

talents was too much above them. You see there was a ratty players, what you call tansy. Yeah. Put all kind of stuff to it. But that made the music hard. You see. That made the other man hard. You couldn't catch on to it. Yeah, couldn't copy it very easily. Couldn't copy it very easily. Couldn't copy it so easily. Some of them pieces he played, you never hear that no more. Yeah. Because they never did write it. Ain't that something? Yeah. And they never hear that. Now if that stuff, if we could have caught it with the tape then, it would have been wonderful to know. And it could have been wrote. You see. And the people had to play it like it was wrote. But outside of that, they had this, now for blues playing, that was, he used to play, Chris Kelly, that was the blues man, could playin' blues. And they say Chris Kelly for blues, that was the man play the blues. This guy could play the blues and make use, you know, play them so fun and sad. And rather jazzy, you know. And that used to draw the crowd at that time, jazz.
Do you remember any of the blues that Chris Kelly used to play? Were they just make up blues or other tunes that you remember?

Well, he used to play so many different blues. I'm telling you the truth. Some blues he used to play, I'd have to take of them. He did some sad blues, you know. Yeah. He used to make so many different, like that piece, what Buddy P.T. used to put in there. Down, down, down, down, down. That was some pretty stuff then. And then fall down low, you know, and get down into blues. You know, it was really wonderful at that time. Did Chris? Of course, if he was here now, I think it would take with this rock and roll, you know. Yeah, I bet they'd like it. They'd still like it. Yeah, they'd see the way he played. It would sound like it. All it would have to be to change was the rhythm section. You know. We'd have to change the beat. That's all on the same number. You see?
That's all.

But otherwise it would sound, it would take over so big if they was here, you know. Because these other fellows, like Pete Burkard, they was reading musicians. You know, they didn't get from here. They're just like a preacher. A preacher at that time was a better preacher than the preachers now for their education. You see what I mean? The preachers then would preach and understand what they're preaching about and they'd just get the words and they wouldn't know how to read it in a book. Now them fellows didn't know nothing. They played it better than the man was reading.
Did you hear much music in the churches? Did you belong to a church in those days? Did you ever go to the churches? Did you hear any of the singing there? What kind of music they had there?
Well, they had a lot of singing in the churches at that time. Brother Bowling's number and stuff like that, you know.
Which church did you go to? Were you Catholic or Protestant or Baptist?
I used to go to all of them, but I was Catholic, but I go to all of them now. Sometimes I fall in the Baptist church and sometimes I used to play in the spiritual church,
you know.
Yes, I know sometimes they have music in there.

Sometimes I used to play the piano in the spiritual church, but then I'd just wait till they sing whatever they sing and pick it up, you see, and go on with them. You see, that's the way I'd do. Of course, they wouldn't have no music. They don't have no music, but I used to go around there when I was kind of, you know, before it got operated on, I used to go play in the churches, you know, and help them out because I haven't been playing much otherwise, but I'd get a job with this, this, now I play mostly with this fellow. He always come get me to play with him going out in the country, you know. They call him Doc. Doc?
That's all I know.

What does he play? No, I don't know. Trumpet, trumpet. He played trumpet. What do you think? He hires his own men. He hires different men all the time to play, but he's a trumpet player. He been playing trumpet quite a while. He plays this Dixieland. And he tries to rock and roll too. He didn't sing, you know. But I've been playing with him off and on.
I was going to ask some more about Chris Kelly. Did he use any mutes or a hat or a derby?
Yeah, he used a flusher, toilet flusher, what you call these flusher.
A rubber plunger then.
A plunger flusher, and he used a mute, wah-wah mute, and he used some other different mute. He had about four or five different mutes, and he used his derby. He had a derby, and he used his derby.
He did change them over while he was playing?

Change them over while he was playing. You see, every time he'd pick up, he'd pick up a different mute. Wow, that's cool. And on the last, before he, when he'd take a hat, he'd use it much, you know, a mute. Different mutes for different pieces.
Did he ever use anything special for going out? Did he use an open horn going out or anything like that on the last chorus?
Well, yeah, most of the time he'd go out with an open horn. Open horn.
Mm-hmm.
How long did those blues last?
Did he play any length of time, or just about how long would they last when he'd play a blues like that? Did he play a long time or short?

Oh yeah, he'd play them a long time, you know, sometimes. He'd play them long, quite long, you know. He'd play them long, put all kind of stuff in it, you know, out his head, you know. And the people would be dancing?
Dancing, yeah.

They'd have a gang. They'd draw a crowd. Well, you see them, at that time, all of them would draw their dick, had their crowd, you see. Some would like him, some would like the other. But I think for blues, they'd draw a bigger crowd with the rough gang, you understand? And that's what it takes to get.
If you want to answer the phone, we can turn this off for a minute.

And for the music you hear now, you don't hear nothing now but this rock and roll, why the changes is not the same as them, you know what I mean? Of course, the changes that we would play music then was harder than now because some of the numbers now which you play is pretty hard for me, you know. Forget right now because Lewis, when I was playing with Landry and Lewis, they used to play some of them numbers that they played and there was some hard for me to catch in, you know what I mean? Because I used to hear them but I never did play them, you see. I mean, they used to pick up and play them but I used to just dance them myself but I never had played them and never had known at that time, you see. Because all I was doing was running bumming with the musicians, you see. That was the Bletchens.
That's what made me pick up and get a chance to play. That was the Bletchens you're talking about when Big Eye Lewis.
Yeah, with Big Eye Lewis, yeah.
Was Ernest Rogers the drummer with you in those days?

Yeah, he was playing there too. I think I worked there four years and Lewis worked there nine years. Yeah, he was. Well, I remember when Walter was there. Mm-hmm. And I taken the job and I stood there until they all left. After Landry left and Big Eye Lewis left, he was running the job, Big Eye Lewis. But after Landry left, well that made us go to another job but didn't last long. We just quit that job and went to another one and it didn't last long. And the man didn't have no money and went under. So that made us, didn't go back. Well, they wanted us back but they wouldn't go so. I wanted to stay down there, me, because I was doing all right down there but they didn't want to stay down there. They didn't want to go back. Well, I wanted to stay down there but they asked me why I wanted to leave. I told them I wanted to leave. I didn't want to leave because I've been there that long and was used to the people. Yeah, where was that other job?
I don't remember.

It was on St. Claude between, between, it was on St. Claude between Two Row and Boiwin. I remember, yeah, Two Row and Boiwin. It was the waiter, his son opened it. Yeah, I think he's a bus driver. Yeah, I never knew that place.
I didn't live here then but I'd come down on vacation. I don't think I ever got there.
Yeah, and so that's the place where we left the job. Otherwise, she didn't want us to leave. Poor thing. She died something about a couple months ago.
Got burnt up.
In that fire, yeah. That was just since Christmas.
I could have went back there but after I got sick I didn't worry about it anymore. I think Sadie was playing there. D.D.
Billy, Billy. Billy and D.D.
Not Sadie, Sadie's sister. I always get them mixed up with Sadie.
Yeah, that's her sister.
Yeah, yeah.
I was going to ask a little bit more about some trumpet players while we were talking about them. Joe Oliver, do you remember, did he use mutes or derby or anything?

Yeah, he used to use different mutes on his trambone. In fact, he used real trombone mutes and he had a flush or two he used to use sometimes on it. Sometimes, them trombone players at that time, they wouldn't move the slide sometimes. They'd just hold it and play trombone like that. That was hard to do. Who's this?
This Oliver and them— Well, Oliver's a cornet player though, wasn't he?
Did you ever hear him on trombone? I never heard him on trombone.
I heard him on trombone. Kid Oakland, I heard him on trombone. Kid Oakland, I heard him on trombone. Kid Oakland, I heard him on trombone.
Kid Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland
Be sure it wasn't Kid Ori you're thinking of. I thought Kid Ori was a trombone player in Hollywood.
Kid Ori, that's the one, Kid Ori. That's Kid Ori, that's right, that's Kid Ori I'm talking about.
He still plays out in California.
Yeah, he's in California. He left here with Lewis, didn't he?
About that time, a little bit before I think even.
You talking about Joe Oliver?
Yeah, Joe Oliver. I just wondered if you heard him, what kind of a mute he used.
Well he used a regular mute. I guess he mixed up with Oliver, the other one. He used a regular mute.
Do you remember Freddie Keppert? He left here very young when you were young.

Yeah, Freddie Keppert, I remember him. The last time I seen him, the last time I seen Freddie Keppert was around at the Corporator's Hall. That was the last job I seen him play. I never heard no more of him. Freddie Keppert went left here or something. I don't know what happened to Freddie Keppert. But that's the only time I seen him once in my life. Before, I never seen him no more.
Freddie Keppert. Do you remember anything about his playing or anything about his band or anything like that?

Oh, I don't know who he, I forgot who he had in his band. I don't remember him so good. I remember him playing at the Corporator's Hall, but I know when Punch and I, Punch and them started playing music, well they used to have all that Punch and.
How was Punch in those days? How did he sound? Was he popular? Yeah, he was popular.
He was pretty good at that time. He was pretty good. Punch and, what you call him? Oh man, oh man, that was goody good at that time.
Who was the other? Oh man. How did Rene sound?
I never got to hear him when he was really good.

He would play a sweet trumpet. He was more of a sweet trombone player. He would play a sweet, kind of a lightish tone. But the rudders had a kind of a little coarse tone. You know what I mean? That was different in the trumpets. To my idea, lots of them had coarse tones and he had a little sweet tone like a blue or something like a cruzut, you know, like a just plain. The tonation was different from the rest. Because here his tone was different from all of them. I never thought they had no tone like him. But that Chris Kelly, that was the blues man. He come over all of the blues, in my opinion.
I wondered which one of those fellas did you work with? You mentioned you worked with Kid Rene.

Oh yeah, I worked with Kid Rene. Last time he asked me to work with him again, I didn't want to work with him. He was playing down on St. Gloria's Street at the, somewhere down there on St. Gloria's Street, near the bridge down there.
Yeah, the place called the Cadillac.
Cadillac, that's right. He wanted me to play there with him. That's before he, you know, before he getting sick. He wasn't so good then, I guess, as in the early days.
He was sort of sick then, I think.
Yeah, he was kind of sick. He was drinking too much, I believe. You see, a lot of times you drink a lot, that would throw you back, you know.
Did you ever play any jobs with Chris Kelly?

Yes, I played a couple of jobs with Chris Kelly. There was a party, you know, house dancing. Used to have dances in the house, like you have a birthday party. Well, that would do your job too, you know, at that time. Because when people would give a birthday party, well, they'd use a band. And it would always be six pieces, you know.
Do you remember anybody else in the band?
In Chris Kelly's band?
In the, yes, Chris Kelly, that he used at that time?

Well, he used a little dad sometimes, a little dad playing banjo. And also he used a guy, a guy used to play the guitar and banjo too. But let me see, and they had Morris Morera too, he played at that time. And Santiago too, Willie Santiago, he played too at that time. They all used to hire them, different band would hire them, you know what I mean?
Remember any clarinets that was with the…

Well, the clarinets they had the Osie Boys and T.U. And, uh, Elisier Ree. And Elisier Ree. Little Cripple Peele, Cripple Peele. And, let's see, Joe Watson. All them clarinets players was playin' at that time.
Do you remember who worked with Chris Kelly? George Boyd.
George Boyd.
George Boyd.
Hmm. George Boyd and Boyd came with Chris Kelly.
Did you ever work with Buddy Petit? Ever play any jobs with Buddy Petit?

Oh no, I never played no jobs with Buddy Petit, but I mostly would be there with him, you know, all the time. I wasn't playin' then when I used to go around with them, but then I used to go around to the dance. I didn't pick it up yet until the late chapter, around after, before World War I. I picked it up a couple of times, a couple of months before World War I.
Who would, who did you like on clarinet? Any favorite players on clarinet?

Well, I used to like, for my clarinet playing, I used to like George Boyd and, and, uh, I think I learned he was good too, he was good at the time, but he was playin' with Manuel, uh, Manuel, uh, Perez. That was his band, he was playin' with the, what's the name of the band again, the Olympia, wasn't it?
I've forgotten now, I believe it's the Olympia.
He was playin' with the Olympia and the Superior. He used to play with all of them, but I mean that was his regular band, Manuel Perez.
I think Manuel had a band they called Imperial sometimes too.
Imperial, yes, that's what I'm talking about, they had the P-Imperial and the Superior. Yeah. . .
We were talking about clarinet players.
To Nicholas too, he was all right, Nicholas. I was, oh Joe Nicholas. Yeah he used to play clarinet too, Wooden Joe. But I played with him several times.
Do you remember hearing Sam Dutre play at all?
I heard him play on the roof garden with the Superior Band.
That before Big Eye played with him?

Yeah, before Big Eye. And I heard him play somewhere else, I can't think of it now, but he used to play mostly with Sam Morgan I believe. Yeah, he played with Sam Morgan. Because that's what I tell you, this rough kind of playing, that was George A. Boyd, I believe he was the roughest one and didn't know nothing about no music and could play the sweet clarinet. He was a big fella, kind of ugly, but he could play a clarinet. And he played with different good bands. All of them was good, but I mean at that time people wanted the jazz, like I say. If you'd do the nicer you'd play, well that was society. You'd play around here at the Frans Ami Hall for the society people because they had the society people at that time and they had the bad people, the ratty people at that time. Well all the nice balls and all that, well they'd hire all them nice bands. That was like Sam Morgan and Superior and all like that, Olympia and all like that. Them kind of bands that hired them, them kind of bands because they wasn't, you know, no ratty. But them other bands for them balls, them the band and the views. But for nice dancers like them people down there one time, them Frans Ami Hall and right here, this Copper Raiders, that was a door, that was a terrible band there. They used to come down here, I used to sit on this same step down there.
Wait, is that the old Halley Perseverance or something?
That's the Hall right there, it's a church now, it's a church now right there. That's the Copper Raiders Hall, that's the, I mean the Perseverance Hall. Perseverance, that's it right there.
Did they ever call that Cooperator's Hall either?
No, they called it Copper Raiders Hall on, uh, uh, uh,
On Liberty. Liberty, sure. That's what I thought. It's a church too now. Yes, it's a Baptist church now.
It's a Baptist church now, so the economy hall is about to say. Yes. And this hall, this is a church too. Co-operated.
This hall.
They made a church out of it. The Perseverance. And the Franz Amis is a church there.
It's over on the next street. Next street on Roberson Street.
Mm-hmm. Between Two Row Round and Ann Boyd.
Did you ever hear any music over, there's a new hall up there on Durbanese Street?
Well I played there a couple of times with George Astute, I played a couple of Bonquets there with George Astute and Joe Nicklaus and that bass player, what's his name again?
I played a couple of times with a couple of times with a drum. I played a drum. I played a drum.

And Dave, Dave, what do you mean? Dave, that's all I know used to play. And Chani, used to play with Chani. I had a job at the last roundup, used to play with Chani and Po Re. I played so many different places at the last roundup, yeah, we used to play there, me and Chani and he's living here, Chani. Yes. I never did get to meet him. I saw him on the street once, about a half a block away somebody pointed him out but I
never did get to talk to him. He used to play with the tuxedo. Yes, Celestan and that group I think. Celestan.

Did you ever work with Celestan at any time? I don't see now. I think, yeah, I worked with Celestan one time, on Liberty at the St. Teresa Hall. Oh yeah. They had a hall build build in the yard. I worked with them there when their first created, when their first first opened. between Jackson and Phillip. I think they ought to be there now. I know they're still down.
Yeah, I remember one big hall. There's a church, one place, used to call it an old Providence Hall, I believe, too, way up there.
Yeah, and then they had the San Suu that was running at that time. We used to play up there, too. I played there at the time, at the San Suu on Howard Street.
I was going to ask about the artesian hall. You know where Big Eye is?
That's where the last place, I played there, too, once or twice, at the San Suu Tidgin Hall upstairs. And I gave a dance there myself and played my own dance with René.
Did they have many dances there in the old days? I never knew many dances in my time.
Oh yeah, yeah, plenty of balls there.
There were?

Yeah, different, but that ball never did take much, because the copyright is in the Hoops Hall, they used to call it. The Hoops Hall, that was it. They called it the copyright, but it's the Hoops Hall. They called it the Hoops Hall, and then they ate, they called it the copyright. But the old times, the Hoops. The Hoops, yeah. And they used to call the other one the Economy Hall. That was always the Economy Hall. Well, they used to kill these places down there, because this hall was so small. The most that they used to have down there was banquets, banquets, you know? Banquets, like in the, they used to have that in the day, you know, on Mondays like that, them societies, like the Artesian Society, the Corporatees and all them societies used to give their ball that day, in the banquet day. Well that was the most they played there, was banquets and weddings and things like that. But the poorest ball, they never would make none of them out of no ball, because I tried to make something out of myself and they wouldn't go. Never did make no money on no dance at the competition. That's where Louis was living.
Yes, I remember that. In those days, when he was living there, I don't remember any balls

or any dances. No, they never had no dances there. They'd have a little wedding like that night, didn't they? They'd have banquets and meetings and things like that, like they have down there right there at this hall down there on Robinson. Robinson and, what's his name, this is John Zami. This is John Zami right there on Robinson and Columbus. That's another hall. Well they have like little dances there now and then
like weddings and stuff like that. They have weddings and things like that, banquets and

things up in there too. Well that's the most that they have. They don't have no dances there, no big dances. And since these big halls, they opened up now, these new halls, but they don't have nowhere else to go but them new halls. They have everything in them one halls. They don't have nowhere for the Dixieland bands to play because it don't take. It don't take no more. It takes some time in the country. Like we played a dance carnival night in Shell Beach. That's way down. Well they had a lot of people there ask for a whole lot of Dixieland numbers. We had to play them. You see like. Who else is with you? This fellow Doc? Doc and Harold Christoff. A saxophone player? Yeah, saxophone player. Harold Christoff and myself and a guitar player. I don't know this guitar player's name. He's coming. But he's pretty good. He's supposed to come here, but he never did come. They said he was supposed
to come. I was supposed to work out with him a couple of pieces. We got a guitar player next

door. He plays the blues sometimes. I was going to ask if you ever worked with Piku, Alphonse Piku. Oh yeah, I played with Piku a couple of times. I played with Piku a couple of times. Alphonse Piku. He still got a place up on the Northside. Yeah. And Robertson, he plays
Sunday night sometime with a little band. He plays? You'll get on the player next. I never
see him. I try to see him. I seen him around there one time. He looks like he's getting so old.

He's getting pretty old, but he doesn't look too well, but he still plays sometime around eight o'clock. He'll play about a half a dozen pieces, you know. Yeah, he got a piano player. With Walter. Walter, you know, the guitar player who works at his bar.

Yeah. Yeah, I know him and the old man. Yeah, I seen him there. Alphonse Piku, yeah. I seen y'all had a funeral there one time. They're playing a funeral, you know, taking a- Oh, that movie and all that made. Yeah, the movie. The television, yes.
That was all right. Four years ago now. Three years ago, anyway.
I was standing on the corner, me and Howard and somebody else.
Well, I guess I saw you over there. I remember seeing Kid Howard and talking to some of the fellas.

Yeah. Yeah. Me and him and Jim Crow. Yeah, that's right. I saw you then. I remember. Because he didn't play in our scene, you know. He was in the band. Sure, I remember now seeing you. I forgot about that. Yeah, in the band. I was talking to Pryju too. I worked with Pryju too. A couple times. You know Willie Pryju. Yes. Cornette player. Yeah. A couple times. And then the trombone player. He used to play trombone and now he plays the bass on. Red.
Red Clark, yeah. Mm-hmm. How did Pryju rank in the old days? Was he considered one of the best ones?

Oh yeah, he was, he had a, say, a cranny like a pipe. Yeah, he still has a little. He had that cranny like a pipe. Yeah, he used to play that drum. Yeah, he used to play. He could play too. Yeah. And him and Louis was good friends. They used to play each other, help each other out around, around Pete Lyle was around there when he was playing there with Marie and Arthur and Benville. Marie and Ben, I was there. I was there. I was there with Marie. I think it is. Over there with Benville.
Yeah, I think that's right. I was there with Benville.

I was there with Benville. I was there with Benville. I was there with Benville. I was there with Benville. I believe it was Bill in there, yeah. No, they tore it down by now. I don't think. I think it's there. It's the grocery there now. And the project hits right into it.
Yeah, it's right across the street.

It looks like it now. That looks like the same building. I think they tore down most of you. Really? Because when I passed there in the bus, I said, that's the building. When I passed there in the St. Bernard bus going uptown, the bus tore in that St. Louis. No, that's right. That's at St. Louis. That street. That's different. That's on St. Louis. Yeah, I think they tore down Pete Lyle. Yeah, they tore down Pete Lyle. That's, this is Frank Marnie's place. That's right. Used to have a van in there too.
It was a parking lot. It might be still a parking lot. Anyway, they tore down most of that.
Yeah, it's a parking lot. I remember now. Most of that street that was torn down. Yeah, that's right.
They tore down, you know, all of that.
Yeah, they tore that down to make that parking lot. That's right.
What did you say, who was the name of that man that ran that place that's still there now? Frank somebody? Frank Paday.
Oh, he ran that place there.

He used to run at that time, you know. Used to have, he's a policeman. Oh, it's close to Lula White's. Yeah, close to Lula White's. That's right. And it's still there now, yeah. It's there, yeah, now, but it's a grocery store.
It's a grocery store. It's a grocery store. Mm-hmm.
What was his name again? I couldn't, I don't, a lot of these names, you know, fresh names.
Frank Paday? He used to run that place. He's a white fellow. How's it spelled?
Police. Paday and Pierre. I don't know how it spelled.
We could look it up. I'm not, I can't, I can't pronounce it.
Yeah, he was a policeman then. I don't know. He was a policeman, yeah. Yeah, he, and then.
Somebody told me once a fellow by the name of Frank Early or someplace.

Frank Early, yeah, he was on, right there too. He was on Liberty and, Liberty and Benville. That's where he was, you know, he used to get so drunk sometimes he used to, didn't know how the automobile used to take him in the place. He used to run that place there.
Somebody told me that Tony Jackson, the piano player and singer played there. Did you ever hear Tony Jackson? I think he left here when you were very young. I thought you might have heard him.

No, I used to know, I knew where he was living at though. He was living around there, right around the corner from there, what I'm talking about. He was living on the corner I think. Corner in Hillary.
Did you ever hear another fellow, Alfred Wilson, a piano player in the district on Basin Street there? It was way back maybe around 1910 to 15 along that period.
Well, Alfred, Alfred William, he was playing with a violin player and a bass and a guitar at that time. Right on the corner, let's see now.
That was a different man I think. This was.
Right. Benville Street. He was playing Benville and Basin. It had a tile front there, that's all gone.
Was that Tom Anderson's place or?
Tom Anderson was on Ramport.
He had a saloon on Iberville and Basin though too I think. I think they had a trio sometimes, string trio with guitar and bass and there.
Yeah, but I don't, I can't think of it. That was Frank Woerley. That was Frank Woerley too. Had that place. That's my knowing as far as I've been.
Along in there.
Frank Woerley had that place too. And Tom Anderson was on Basin Street on Ramport Street.
I know he had just down for the Tencent Storys, I think he had one place.

Yeah, that's where he had a place. Yeah, a big place because Louis, my cousin was Louis Prevost, you know. Oh yeah. He used to play a clarinet and then he was playing with a lyric, playing trumpet. But I used to go sit up there and sit up there with him and eat and drink up there when, at Tom Anderson when Louis Armstrong was playing up there. Cause he used to come bring his cornet. My cousin used to put the clarinet in his pocket. Two pieces in there. Two pieces in each pocket and go up there and play. And I used to go up there with him, he used to go up there every night. Cause he was living with me then, rooming on St. Claude and Dumaine. Still and still there, yeah. He was rooming there with me. And I used to go there every night on Grandpa Street by him, playing with Tom Anderson upstairs there. And he was playing up there. Sometimes George and Boyd. The cabaret was upstairs. Yeah, upstairs, like the economy hall. Like this hall here at the bandstand, upstairs. Just like people got that stand at the place basically.
Oh, just the bandstand was up high.

Yeah, the bandstand was up high. People used to dance down. The cabaret was on the first floor. The cabaret was on the first floor. The bandstand was up looking down on the floor. Yeah. They got that carnival, that club uptown got the bandstand like that. Cause I played up there a couple of years ago. Up there, the club up there on, you know, Irish Channel, big club, carnival club. They got a bandstand upstairs. They got a beautiful club up there.
What street is that on?
That's on, that's on, uh, Nunciation I think. Nunciation Street.
Nunciation.
Mm-hmm. We lived there one time.
I don't remember that club. There was one hall there where the Buzzards have, they used to have dances where Joe Avery used to play.
Yeah, he did too.

But the bandstand wasn't up high. I don't know that club you're talking about then. On the Nunciation you think? I'd like to take a picture of it sometime. There's another club on Magazine Street I think is still there.
Magazine Street too, yeah. They got a lot of different clubs up there but that's where I used to play it. I played once or twice different dances, you know.
Was it up above Jackson on Nunciation Street then?
Yeah, it's up above there.
Yeah, probably there. It was a big hall I remember.

Yeah, it's a big hall with a big bandstand up there cause I know we had to cram up the stairs to go up there, you know. Most of the halls that they were in the hall, the hall that they built in was the bandstand was way up. It would be better for you, you know what I mean? Cause right on the floor you'd be in the way of the people and you'd be up there out the way, you see. Music would sound better. It's a mile out there, you know. Because that's the way the old time halls used to have the bandstand up. If I was to have a hall that's where I'd put my bandstand upstairs and let them look down on the public.
Did it get sorta hot up there sometime though?
Well no, it wasn't hot up there. Yeah, sometime it got hot at the carburetors cause you're so close to the ceiling.
Yeah, that's what that was. And over here at Artesian Hall too.

Well, Artesian Hall too, that bandstand railing, well they did have a bigger, right here they had a bigger, you know, place for the band up there, a bigger gallery. But right here they had like a little gallery, wide as my gallery out there. I've never been in the Perseverance Hall. What does it look like inside the Perseverance?
Is that old balcony still there for the bandstand? Did they tear that out?
No, I believe they threw that out. I never been in there. I never knew the sense I've been in. I went in there one day in the church. I never knew it.

The Economy Hall still has the big bandstand. We took some pictures of that. Yeah. Like in the old days, it's still there. And of course Artesian Hall is the same. I believe they got it up there yet. I wondered about Perseverance if it's up there.
I believe it's up there yet, but they made the altar there. You know, they blocked it off, I believe. It's nothing there now, but the altar's there.
What was Franz and Me Hall like in the old days? Was the, did they have a high bandstand up high?

Franz and Me Hall? Yeah, they had a whole upstate. The whole bandstand up there. The bandstand up there. Most all the halls had it. The New Hall, the phones I mean. The New Hall was too. Yeah, bandstand up there.
I think New Hall is all torn out now. I remember there one day they were having some games in there.
Yeah, they had a keynote game. Keno or something. Yeah.

I went in there one time, but I didn't see any bandstand. I was going to ask a little bit about some of the parades. I don't suppose you ever played any parades. Did you? Any instrument? No, I never had the chance to play any parade.

Like a brass instrument or drums or anything? No, I never had played anything like that. No, I never had played. But I was supposed to play a drum, but I never did play it because the drum players showed up. I never did like the parade so much. Did you ever follow them when you were a boy? Yeah, I used to run behind them. I used to follow them a lot, run behind them, just like the second line. No, I used to second line, run behind them the same way I do now, but they was, you know, it sounded different than they sound now. It was a bigger band or something. I don't know. It wasn't as much. I don't know. It looked like they played more music then than they play now. I don't understand. It looked like they was the most strong or something like that at the time. But I noticed the funerals down there now look like they played more Saturday. Of course, they might have used more trumpets and more clarinets, you see. I believe they used two or three clarinets at that time. And they had alto and all of that then, you know? Yeah. Alto and flute and all that during that time. That made the parade sound more indifferent because I remember when the art fellas paraded and all that time, because I made a parade with them when I was on the horse then. When the art fellas paraded the last, when they gave that picnic at the fairground, we had two bands. And they had big bands and they played the brass band and the string band. We had, I think we had Kid René and we had the Superior Band.
Did they have dancing out there then too?

At the fairground? Oh yeah, they had dancing like this. When bands stopped, the other one would play. And they made the people keep on dancing because when this band would stop, they'd run to the next band and dance there. Did the brass band play for dancing too?
The brass band played for dancing and the string band too, you see.
But it was such a big band, they had a big band standing there. The band stands full. It ain't two, three pieces that they use now.
What do you mean by the string band? How many instruments? What kind of instruments were in it?
Well the string band, the string band had bass violin and banjo and clarinet and cornet. Six pieces.
Yeah, trombone too? Some... Trombone.

Yeah, Rector Dance Band. Yeah, the dance band, that was the string band. But the brass band had a lot of brass. They had no bass violin and they never had no guitar. They just had trombones, cornet and clarinet, saxophone, I mean clarinet and you know so forth.
Yes, regular brass.

All regular brass. Everything brass, no string at all. But they played for dancing too. They played to dance too, you see, at that time. It was a string, a brass band wouldn't go much for a dance now, you know. No, they don't use them now. It wouldn't go. But them time it went too. Yeah. But they didn't like it as much as they did the string band. Mm-hmm. Because the string band gets your jazz more better, but there's as much a jazz band and the brass band played more marches like that.
Did they call them jazz bands then or what did they call them? Just the jazz bands?
Yeah, they called them jazz bands.
Oh, jazz bands.
When did you first hear that word, the jazz? When did they start using that, do you know?

Well, they used to say, kid punch jazz band on the program, you know, when they advertised the band at that time. Yeah. You see, kid punchin' his jazz boys or kid punchin' his jazz band. But sometime if Rainier's band wasn't playing, well, sometimes they'd use Raymond Rainier's men because men were so short at that time. Sometime when Sam Morgan would get short, well, he'd use some of them men when they wasn't playing. But when they was playing, well, they had to use what they could at that time because they didn't have the musicians they have today. No. Quite natural in the time the musicians were scarce. But now they're plentiful. See, that makes the world hard for musicians now.

Well, I was going to ask in the very beginning about if you ever had any lessons on the piano. You said that Rene and people helped you some. Oh, yeah. Did you ever take lessons on the piano with a book and a picture?
Yeah, I took lessons in first grade and second grade.
Who was your teacher?
Well, I took it lately, you know.
Oh, and just in late, late, not when you were a little boy.
I was just a jazz man.
You just picked it up.

Just picked it up. Just picked it up like this. They went on and played and hang around them until I learned. And went on and played different jazz with them. Well, first time, you know, you get cold feet and just kept on until I learned. Sure. But sometime I'd go there and the pieces I could play, well, they'd play for me to catch on and that's how I come on. So that's how I got to learn. And Raffaella and them, I liked it and everywhere they'd go, I'd go. Everywhere I'd know they got to dance, I'd run behind them until I learned how to play.
Do you remember any of them?

I made a lot of money at it because, you know, me enjoying the time because I was getting the money and they was helping me out. I played pretty good at that time, you know, the jazz. But now the music has changed so you got to try to follow the crowd now, you know. Play the move. It's not complicated now as it's been done because the music was so hard then, you see. Of course you didn't have to do but complement and the way you complement then was different than when you complement now. Because the banjo was hitting. See that was the complement and you all you had to do is hit with the banjo then. So just hit cards the same way you would.
Hit cards.

Make cards like that but now they make cards. Boom, boom, boom, boom. Boom, boom, boom. That's the kind of card now. But them time you make. Like that. It's playing cards. It's playing cards. Hit like you.
It's playing cards.
It's playing cards. Like your plug and something at that time, you see. And that's what they wanted, the chords, the heavy chords.
Did you ever play many piano solos in the old days in the band? Did they ever take a solo on the piano or anything?
Well, yeah, I take a solo sometimes. Yeah, I take a solo. I mean, in the old days.
They give you a solo. A long time ago did they do that ever?

Yeah, they give you a solo to play. They give you a solo all the time. You know, take down and give a rest until they come up and go out. Quite naturally, there's a lot of things, you know what I mean? You had to do them that destroyed on you what you could take it or not. Make you play. See, that made you make a musician. That would make you scared to let the public would hear what you're making. If you wasn't playing, you had to play the right stuff. Otherwise, people wouldn't think you're playing. But now you can make anything, but people go for it, you see. That's the different nature of people today. But then time, if you make a false chord, well, you just did look at you and frown, the rest of the musicians, you know. You would feel cheap. They'd make you feel cheap, you know what I mean? When you'd get on, they wouldn't bother with you, nothing like that, at that time. But now the more worse you play, the better they like. So you don't know how to do now. That's right.
You get up there and make nothing and ho, oh, and then that's going to take.
That'll sell. That'll sell. And you play something beautiful, they don't want that. See? That's the trouble.
Yes, that would be kind of difficult to be playing all night long and scared to make a wrong chord or anything and make it a lot harder, I'd imagine, in those days.

Well, yeah, you'd always try, you see, at that time, because you knew they was going to try to, you, it was going to ignore you, you know. So you'd always try to make as closer to them chords as you could, see. Of course, sometime he'd play better than the other fella, like they had a couple of good piano players here then at that time, you know, was playing around here. Well, sometime, like Ray Batiste, well, he could play in one key. You see, lots of them fellas could play in one key. Well, that, them fellas that play in one key would have a bad show, because they couldn't play in no other way but in that C or that C sharp, some playing in F sharp, C sharp and F sharp. Well, then a lot of bands wouldn't play that.
Yeah, they couldn't play in brass and-

Some of them would pick it up in air natural for you. You see what I mean? Well, that would make you sound, you know, you couldn't get in there harder because you know you ain't been playing nothing in that air natural. Quite naturally, they hardly play in them keys now, you know. First you play in some guitar with a guitar, he'll have to pick it up in air natural or something like that. But in these places, these pieces now, you'll have to pick up in any key, see. And so he said, he don't know where he's playing, he said, where he's playing? He said, I don't know. I'm just playing. I said, where you playing? I said, I don't know where to go. He said, I don't know. I said, well, just go ahead on and play. I guess I got to find you. See? Well, that's the way you play now. But them times they tell you, here's right. Oh, you're gone. See? They're gone. That's the way they play then. But now they don't answer nothing. You just pick up where they play. And they don't know, some of them.
When they, when you, when you start a key, did the leader stump off for you? Yeah, he stumped.
He started, started off.
How'd he stump off? He's done.
And he gone, see. Two, two. Two. Sometimes it's three. You know what that mean? One, two, three. Waltz. A little fast.
Oh yeah.
For a waltz.
Yeah. Did you play many waltzes in the old days? Oh yeah.

Played plenty waltzes. Yeah, played plenty waltzes. That's all they mostly used to play, pretty waltzes. And especially these halls down there. Well, in the coppery's in the economy hall, that used to take too. You had to play waltzes. But on the late watch, when it's getting late, around 12 o'clock, play waltzes. They want to clap it back. That time they play waltzes over three, four times. Because some of the people, they want some nice waltzes sometime. But now they don't care. You can play waltzes now. They talk about you. You can play waltzes. Of course, you go up to country and some of them plays where the older people is, where they have dancers, they love to play to hear the whole same old band, the same old waltzes, you see. Some people don't want you to do, but the teenagers just sitting down and going to sleep. Well, that makes you don't have no show with the teenagers. But you're just good with the old, the older people. But you got to get in with the teenagers now. Them the ones that gives the partisan thing. If you don't play for them, nah, they don't. They sit up and look at you. That's all. They ain't no dang. Now we played a place over in Urode that had a good band. It was a Dixieland on rap. But we played there. I don't think I'm going to go back there in the movie. They wasn't charging but the dialing cord to come in and they said the music was all right swell, but that ain't our type of music. You see? That's what they do. Well, we know we was praying, but they was praying what they knew. They couldn't pray nothing else. But I had to pick up some kind of stuff on there, you see. Make it sound good. And then get us to sing. They had a singer and I just played with the singer. But they didn't have to play much. And me and the singer and the drum, bass, that's all they wanted. They read it that in the whole band. Yeah, yeah. That's why they hardly use a trumpet today. You take that piano and the guitar and the bass or a bass drum and a saxophone and you don't need nothing else if you got a singer. You can make it anywhere with that. They ain't looking for no big pile of music.
Nah.
You see? But them time they wanted to see all that music there. If you didn't have that band there, you didn't have no band.
No two-three pieces. Did you have any singers at all, hadn't in the old days?

Well, most of the band, people would sing with the band, the man who'd lead, you see. The trumpet player and sometimes the guitar player. Sometimes the piano player, he'd sing what he know about a number. That's how it went. But they never had no regular singers unless you go to the entertainers when they had to have, and then you had to be a first class musician to play in the entertainer because they used to, sometimes the singers would put the music on. You take like Buddy Pitti and them brothers, they wouldn't play in that, you know, unless they had a reading man with them. Well, if you play a job with a band and didn't have no reading, and you as a trumpet player didn't know a note, and you as a clarinet player didn't have a note, and the trombone player didn't know a note, well then you didn't have nobody to pick up on that stuff. But if you had a clarinet player to pick it up, well you could go on with him. If you had a saxophone player also to pick it up, well the trumpet player could go on with him. That's what they'd make a pretty second behind him, and he could play too. See? But you take them time, if you had to have one man and a couple of men in the band read, because the trumpets hardly know, like them fellas, you know, Chris Ketner, they never had no kind of music. But still in all they made money at that time. And they got them jobs every Saturday and Sunday and on the week they was working all the time. They didn't have nothing to do, they didn't do nothing but that. And they could, you know, they had enough money to have a good time in the day, they didn't have nothing to do. And that night go to work, they had big dinners, and all of them be around the table for the big dinners and rent in this yard, they had a big yard. All of them would get around, all of them punch, all of them musicians would come there and get around the table and eat car, where are they all on Monday, see? Because they'd play so hard on Fridays and Saturdays and Sunday like that. At that time, and sometime in the week, and at some time they'd have weddings and things, they'd play all such as things like hall, like the cops like to St. Giles, what you call that, that cut like hall there, or St. Catron, where they used to play all in there too, you see? So them halls used to have them going because they had plenty of places to play. And for the bands they had then, they didn't have much, they had a lot of halls and no bands, you see? Then, at that time, because they had, look at the halls they had, now look at the halls we got now to play. See, different? I mean, look at the bands we got, we ain't got no place to play.
